objectives: Name types of angle and measure them with a protractor
Use angle facts on a straight line, round a point and for vertically opposite angles
Use corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles on parallel lines
reviewNotes: The figure is schematic; angle marks are not drawn to scale with arcs.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Types of angle
blocks.md: An angle measures a turn. An **acute** angle is less than 90°, a **right** angle is exactly 90°, an **obtuse** angle is between 90° and 180°, a **straight** angle is 180° and a **reflex** angle is between 180° and 360°. Two angles are **complementary** if they add up to 90° and **supplementary** if they add up to 180°.

blocks.title: Angle facts
blocks.md:
- Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
- Angles round a point add up to 360°.
- **Vertically opposite** angles (made by two crossing lines) are equal.
- Check measuring: place the centre of the protractor on the vertex and read the scale that starts at 0° on one arm.

blocks.caption: Two crossing lines: the four angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°.
blocks.alt: Two lines crossing; opposite angles equal 65 and 115 degrees.

blocks.title: Parallel lines
blocks.md: A line crossing two parallel lines makes: **corresponding** angles (F shape) that are equal; **alternate** angles (Z shape) that are equal; **co-interior** angles (C or U shape) that add up to 180°. These rules only work when the lines are parallel.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Reading the wrong scale on the protractor: an obtuse angle cannot be 40°.
- Using Z or F rules on lines that are not parallel.
- Forgetting that co-interior angles add up to 180° but are not equal.

blocks.title: Example 1: straight line
blocks.statement: Three angles on a straight line are x, 2x + 10 and 3x + 20 (in degrees). Find x and the angles.
steps: The angles add up to 180°: x + 2x + 10 + 3x + 20 = 180.
The angles are 25°, 60° and 95°. Check: 25 + 60 + 95 = 180.

blocks.title: Example 2: crossing lines
blocks.statement: Two straight lines cross and one angle is 65°. Find the other three angles.
steps: The angle next to it is on a straight line: 180° − 65° = 115°.
The angle vertically opposite 65° is also 65°.
The angle vertically opposite 115° is also 115°.

lessons.title: Triangles and quadrilaterals

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Classify triangles by sides and by angles
Use the angle sum of a triangle and the exterior angle property
Name the special quadrilaterals and their properties
Use the angle sum of a quadrilateral
reviewNotes: Some textbooks define a trapezium as having at least one pair of parallel sides, others exactly one; confirm the local convention.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Triangles
blocks.md: A triangle has three sides and three angles that **add up to 180°**. By sides: **equilateral** (3 equal sides, all angles 60°), **isosceles** (2 equal sides and the two angles opposite them equal), **scalene** (no equal sides). By angles: acute, right (one angle 90°) or obtuse (one angle over 90°). The **exterior angle** of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

blocks.title: Quadrilaterals
blocks.md: The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°. A **square** has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. A **rectangle** has opposite sides equal and 4 right angles. A **parallelogram** has opposite sides parallel and equal. A **rhombus** has 4 equal sides. A **trapezium** has one pair of parallel sides. A **kite** has two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

blocks.caption: Triangle ABC with angles 50°, 60° and x = 70°.
blocks.alt: A triangle with angles 50 and 60 degrees at the base and x at the top.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking a square is not a rectangle; a square is a special rectangle and a special rhombus.
- Forgetting that the two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
- Using 360° for a triangle or 180° for a quadrilateral.

blocks.title: Example 1: triangle angles
blocks.statement: In triangle ABC, angle A = 50° and angle B = 60°. Find angle C. Then find the angles of an isosceles triangle whose apex angle is 40°.
steps: In the isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal: (180° − 40°) ÷ 2 = 70°.
So its angles are 40°, 70°, 70°.

blocks.title: Example 2: quadrilateral
blocks.statement: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 100° and 120°. Find the fourth. Then find all the angles of a parallelogram with one angle of 80°.
steps: The four angles add up to 360°: 80 + 100 + 120 = 300, so the fourth angle is 60°.
In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal, so another angle is 80°.
Neighbouring angles add up to 180°, so the other two are 100° each. Check: 80 + 100 + 80 + 100 = 360.

objectives: Construct a triangle given three sides
Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line
Construct the bisector of an angle
reviewNotes: The figure shows complete circles instead of arcs for clarity; construction marks in an exam are arcs only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Perpendicular bisector
blocks.md: To bisect the segment AB: set the compasses to **more than half** of AB. Draw an arc above and below from A, then the same arcs from B. Join the two crossing points with a ruler. This line cuts AB at its midpoint M at 90°. Every point on it is the same distance from A and from B.

blocks.title: Angle bisector and a 60° angle
blocks.md: To bisect an angle at O: draw an arc that cuts both arms; from those two points draw equal arcs that cross inside the angle; join O to the crossing. To make **60°**: from A draw an arc of any radius cutting the base at P; with the same radius, centre P, cut the arc at Q; join A to Q. Bisect that to get 30°.

blocks.caption: Perpendicular bisector of AB made with two pairs of arcs.
blocks.alt: Two circles centred on A and B crossing; a vertical line through the crossing points meets AB at M.

blocks.title: Triangle with three sides
blocks.md: To construct a triangle with sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm: draw the longest side AB = 7 cm. With compasses at A and radius 5 cm draw an arc; with compasses at B and radius 4 cm draw another arc. The arcs cross at C. Join AC and BC. Never rub out the arcs.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Changing the compass setting between the two arcs of a bisector: use the same radius.
- Setting the radius to **less than half** of AB: the arcs will not cross.
- Measuring with a ruler instead of using arcs when a construction is asked: show all construction marks.

blocks.title: Example 1: perpendicular bisector
blocks.statement: AB = 8 cm. Describe how to find the point equidistant from A and B on a road map, and state the distance AM.
steps: Open the compasses to 5 cm (more than 4 cm, half of AB).
Draw arcs from A and from B above and below AB; join the crossing points.
The line crosses AB at M, the midpoint, so AM = 4 cm.
blocks.answer: **M is at 4 cm from A; the bisector is at 90° to AB.**

blocks.title: Example 2: triangle
blocks.statement: Describe the construction of triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 4 cm. Is it possible?
steps: Check: 5 + 4 = 9 is more than 7, so the arcs will cross: a triangle exists.
Draw AB = 7 cm; arc radius 5 cm from A; arc radius 4 cm from B.
Mark the crossing point C and join AC and BC.
blocks.answer: **Possible; C is where the two arcs meet.**

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the area formulas for the rectangle, square, triangle, parallelogram and trapezium
Convert between units of length and area
Solve practical problems on land and floors
reviewNotes: Circle circumference and area are taught in Form 2 in this scheme; adjust if the official scheme differs.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Area formulas
blocks.md: The **perimeter** is the distance round a shape. The **area** is the surface it covers, in square units:
blocks.tex: A_{\text{rectangle}} = l \times w \qquad A_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2} b h \qquad A_{\text{parallelogram}} = b h

blocks.title: Trapezium
blocks.md: For a trapezium with parallel sides a and b and height h (the distance between them):

blocks.caption: A trapezium plot with parallel sides 30 m and 50 m and height 20 m.
blocks.alt: A trapezium with its top side 30 m, bottom 50 m and a dashed height of 20 m.

blocks.title: Units
blocks.md: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm². 1 hectare = 10 000 m². Use the same unit for all measurements before calculating. The **height** is always at right angles to the base, not along a slanted side.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the slanted side instead of the perpendicular height.
- Forgetting the ½ in the area of a triangle or trapezium.
- Writing area in cm instead of cm², or converting 1 m² to 100 cm² instead of 10 000 cm².

blocks.title: Example 1: rectangle and floor tiles
blocks.statement: A classroom floor at Kumba is 6 m by 5 m. Square tiles of side 50 cm cost 450 FCFA each. How many tiles are needed and what do they cost?
steps: Floor area = 6 × 5 = 30 m² = 300 000 cm²... use 600 cm × 500 cm = 300 000 cm².

blocks.title: Example 2: trapezium
blocks.statement: A plot of land at Bamenda is a trapezium with parallel sides 30 m and 50 m, 20 m apart. Find its area.
steps: Use A = ½ (a + b) × h with a = 30, b = 50 and h = 20.
The area is 800 m².
